Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/

date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1204.002

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/

[LLM] Ghost CMS Content API SQL injection (CVE-2026-26980) admin key theft Exploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated SQL injection against the Ghost CMS Content API endpoint used in CVE-2026-26980 to read the Admin API key and poison articles. Targets the /ghost/api/*content* path carrying SQL keywords in the query string against web-server access logs. Rationale: Pivots on the exact CVE-2026-26980 attack surface — the Ghost Content API path (/ghost/api/.../content) combined with SQLi tokens in the query string — rather than a generic WAF SQLi rule. Cross-checked XLab and BleepingComputer write-ups confirming the unauthenticated Content API read primitive. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.xlab.qianxin.com/ghost-cms-mass-compromised-via-cve-2026-26980-now-fueling-clickfix-attacks/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ghost-cms-sql-injection-flaw-exploited-in-large-scale-clickfix-campaign/

 | project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, Path = csUriStem, Query = csUriQuery, Status = scStatus, UserAgent = csUserAgent, Src = "W3CIISLog"),

[LLM] Endpoint contacts Ghost-poisoning ClickFix loader/TDS/C2 domains Command & Control High
Hunts any internal host resolving or connecting to the Ghost ClickFix campaign's loader, Adspect cloaking/TDS, and Electron C2 domains (clo4shara.xyz, com-apps.cc, web-telegram.ug, etc.) or the staging IP 144.31.236.66. These indicators span the JavaScript loader fetch, fake-CAPTCHA delivery, and Grape Electron beacon. Rationale: Direct IOC sweep on the campaign's named loader/cloaking/C2 domains and staging IP, all confirmed across XLab and BleepingComputer. com-apps.cc added because Cloudflare blocked clo4shara.xyz and the actor rotated to it. Schema fix: Sentinel side now reads DnsEvents.Name/ClientIP and unions CommonSecurityLog for the IP indicator (DnsEvents has no IPAddresses column). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.xlab.qianxin.com/ghost-cms-mass-compromised-via-cve-2026-26980-now-fueling-clickfix-attacks/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ghost-cms-sql-injection-flaw-exploited-in-large-scale-clickfix-campaign/

[LLM] ClickFix Run-dialog chain: explorer-spawned shell fetching ZIP dropper Delivery High
Hunts the ClickFix fake-CAPTCHA pasted-command pattern where explorer.exe (the Windows Run dialog) spawns cmd/powershell/mshta/curl that downloads a ZIP from the campaign domains or pulls a remote archive. This is the hands-on-keyboard-by-victim execution that bridges the poisoned web page to the local payload. Rationale: Anchors on the article's described ClickFix mechanics — a command pasted into the Windows Run dialog (parent=explorer.exe) that drops/extracts a ZIP — paired with the campaign C2 domains, which is far more specific than a generic explorer-spawns-shell rule. Distinct from the excluded encoded-PowerShell/Office-macro rules because the parent is the Run dialog and the predicate is the ZIP+domain combo. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.xlab.qianxin.com/ghost-cms-mass-compromised-via-cve-2026-26980-now-fueling-clickfix-attacks/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ghost-cms-sql-injection-flaw-exploited-in-large-scale-clickfix-campaign/

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"

| order by Timestamp desc

[LLM] Ghost ClickFix payload execution: known hashes / UtilifySetup.exe Electron dropper Installation High
Alerts on execution or file-write of the campaign's confirmed payload hashes (DLL loaders / JS droppers) and the UtilifySetup.exe Inno Setup installer that drops the modified Grape Electron client. High-fidelity IOC match on the final-stage malware. Rationale: Hard IOC match on the five MD5s + SHA1 published by XLab and the UtilifySetup.exe Electron sample (named in XLab/BleepingComputer), making this an alerting-grade detection on the final dropped payload. Hash + named-binary precision keeps FPs near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.xlab.qianxin.com/ghost-cms-mass-compromised-via-cve-2026-26980-now-fueling-clickfix-attacks/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ghost-cms-sql-injection-flaw-exploited-in-large-scale-clickfix-campaign/

[LLM] Grape Electron client persistence via HKCU Run key (setLoginItemSettings) Installation Medium
Hunts the modified Grape desktop (Electron) client establishing persistence by writing an HKCU CurrentVersion\Run value pointing to UtilifySetup/Grape, the behavior of its setLoginItemSettings call. This is the autostart that survives reboot and re-launches the 30-second C2 beacon to web-telegram.ug. Rationale: Targets the article/XLab-described setLoginItemSettings persistence, which in practice writes an HKCU Run value pointing at the Grape/UtilifySetup Electron binary — a registry pivot distinct from the network and process UCs. The UtilifySetup/Grape value-data tokens keep it campaign-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.xlab.qianxin.com/ghost-cms-mass-compromised-via-cve-2026-26980-now-fueling-clickfix-attacks/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ghost-cms-sql-injection-flaw-exploited-in-large-scale-clickfix-campaign/
ATT&CKT1547.001

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9434fe686801742ef7d6da248fb0b900dc32208a", "5659292833ec421da11ebde005d9c9a8", "d30cc10d54ebc967c8538ff74f442eee", "18a7251ddde77ed24bc54700d84d9be1", "f280e12f51f996dae7fffc64a56ee527", "fceca579efcef09eb507c6ca977ea281") or SHA1 in~ ("9434fe686801742ef7d6da248fb0b900dc32208a", "5659292833ec421da11ebde005d9c9a8", "d30cc10d54ebc967c8538ff74f442eee", "18a7251ddde77ed24bc54700d84d9be1", "f280e12f51f996dae7fffc64a56ee527", "fceca579efcef09eb507c6ca977ea281") or MD5 in~ ("9434fe686801742ef7d6da248fb0b900dc32208a", "5659292833ec421da11ebde005d9c9a8", "d30cc10d54ebc967c8538ff74f442eee", "18a7251ddde77ed24bc54700d84d9be1", "f280e12f51f996dae7fffc64a56ee527", "fceca579efcef09eb507c6ca977ea281")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9434fe686801742ef7d6da248fb0b900dc32208a", "5659292833ec421da11ebde005d9c9a8", "d30cc10d54ebc967c8538ff74f442eee", "18a7251ddde77ed24bc54700d84d9be1", "f280e12f51f996dae7fffc64a56ee527", "fceca579efcef09eb507c6ca977ea281") or SHA1 in~ ("9434fe686801742ef7d6da248fb0b900dc32208a", "5659292833ec421da11ebde005d9c9a8", "d30cc10d54ebc967c8538ff74f442eee", "18a7251ddde77ed24bc54700d84d9be1", "f280e12f51f996dae7fffc64a56ee527", "fceca579efcef09eb507c6ca977ea281") or MD5 in~ ("9434fe686801742ef7d6da248fb0b900dc32208a", "5659292833ec421da11ebde005d9c9a8", "d30cc10d54ebc967c8538ff74f442eee", "18a7251ddde77ed24bc54700d84d9be1", "f280e12f51f996dae7fffc64a56ee527", "fceca579efcef09eb507c6ca977ea281")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9434fe686801742ef7d6da248fb0b900dc32208a", "5659292833ec421da11ebde005d9c9a8", "d30cc10d54ebc967c8538ff74f442eee", "18a7251ddde77ed24bc54700d84d9be1", "f280e12f51f996dae7fffc64a56ee527", "fceca579efcef09eb507c6ca977ea281"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

2026-05-25 11 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Lazarus Deploys RemotePE Memory-Only RAT Against Financial and Crypto Firms
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Lazarus DPAPILoader masquerading as Iassvc.dll loaded from non-System32 path

[LLM] Lazarus DPAPILoader masquerading as Iassvc.dll loaded from non-System32 path Installation High
Hunts the RemotePE first-stage loader (DPAPILoader), which ships as a DLL named 'Iassvc.dll' to impersonate the legitimate Windows Internet Authentication Service library and is side-loaded from a writable, non-standard directory. The genuine Iassvc.dll only ever lives under System32/WinSxS, so an Iassvc.dll loaded or written elsewhere is the loader. Rationale: Anchored on the exact DPAPILoader artifact name 'Iassvc.dll' from the article cross-checked against Fox-IT's writeup; the legitimate Iassvc.dll (IAS service) only resides in System32, so a copy/load from any other path is high-fidelity for the side-load with near-zero benign collision. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.fox-it.com/2025/09/01/three-lazarus-rats-coming-for-your-cheese/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/lazarus-group-expands-malware-arsenal.html • https://socprime.com/blog/detect-lazarus-attacks-using-three-new-rats/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "iassvc.dll"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\"
    and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64\"
    and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "iassvc.dll"
| where TargetFilePath !has @"\Windows\System32\"
    and TargetFilePath !has @"\Windows\SysWOW64\"
    and TargetFilePath !has @"\Windows\WinSxS\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DPAPILoader Iassvc.dll Masquerade Loaded From Non-System32 Path

description: Detects a DLL named Iassvc.dll (Lazarus RemotePE DPAPILoader) being loaded from a directory other than the legitimate System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS locations, indicating DLL side-loading and name masquerading.
references:

#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\iassvc\.dll$/i
| NOT TargetFileName=/\\(System32|SysWOW64|WinSxS)\\/i

[LLM] RemotePELoader HTTP C2 beacon to aes-secure.net Command & Control Medium
Hunts the RemotePELoader second stage contacting its command-and-control server 'aes-secure[.]net' over HTTP to fetch and execute the memory-only RemotePE core module. Because RemotePE is never written to disk, this network callout is one of the few durable artifacts of the intrusion. Rationale: Uses the exact C2 domain aes-secure[.]net named in the primary article; the loader chain (DPAPI-loaded RemotePELoader beaconing over HTTP for a memory-only stage) is corroborated by Fox-IT, but the specific domain surfaced only in the primary article — hence Medium confidence; treat as a watchlist IOC and confirm against the Fox-IT IOC table. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.fox-it.com/2025/09/01/three-lazarus-rats-coming-for-your-cheese/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/lazarus-group-expands-malware-arsenal.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "aes-secure.net" or RemoteUrl endswith "aes-secure.net"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "aes-secure.net"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DnsResponseCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: RemotePELoader C2 Callout to aes-secure.net
id: b2e7d40c-1a93-4f6e-8d52-3c0a9f7e6b18
description: Detects DNS resolution of the Lazarus RemotePE command-and-control domain aes-secure.net used by RemotePELoader to fetch the memory-only RemotePE payload over HTTP.
references:

  - https://blog.fox-it.com/2025/09/01/three-lazarus-rats-coming-for-your-cheese/
author: SOC Detection Engineering

tags:

  - attack.t1105
logsource:
  category: dns
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|endswith: 'aes-secure.net'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:(*aes-secure.net OR *AES-SECURE.NET)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName=/aes-secure\.net$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query="*aes-secure.net" by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query="*aes-secure.net" by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
[LLM] RemotePE/PondRAT seven-pass file overwrite then rename and delete (anti-forensic wipe) Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the distinctive secure-deletion routine shared by RemotePE, PondRAT and POOLRAT: each target file is overwritten with constant bytes seven times, then renamed, then deleted. This surfaces as a single process performing many repeated writes to the same path followed by a rename/delete of that path. Rationale: Targets the article's specific anti-forensic signature — seven constant-byte overwrites followed by rename-then-delete, explicitly tied to RemotePE/PondRAT/POOLRAT — expressed as a high-write-count-then-delete threshold per process+file; behavioral/threshold-based, so no single-event Sigma is emitted. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.fox-it.com/2025/09/01/three-lazarus-rats-coming-for-your-cheese/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/lazarus-group-expands-malware-arsenal.html
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileRenamed","FileDeleted")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize Modifies = countif(ActionType == "FileModified"),
            Renames = countif(ActionType == "FileRenamed"),
            Deletes = countif(ActionType == "FileDeleted"),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
        by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256,
           InitiatingProcessId, FolderPath, FileName
| where Modifies >= 7 and (Renames >= 1 or Deletes >= 1)   // 7-pass constant-byte overwrite then rename/delete (RemotePE/PondRAT/POOLRAT secure-wipe)
| order by Modifies desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileDeleted")
| summarize Writes = countif(EventType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")),
            Renames = countif(EventType == "FileRenamed"),
            Deletes = countif(EventType == "FileDeleted"),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
        by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId, TargetFilePath
| where Writes >= 7 and (Deletes >= 1 or Renames >= 1)   // 7-pass overwrite then rename/delete secure-wipe
| order by Writes desc
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId, TargetFileName], function=count(as=writes))
| writes >= 7
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count(eval(Filesystem.action="modified")) as modifies count(eval(Filesystem.action="deleted")) as deletes count(eval(Filesystem.action="renamed")) as renames min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where modifies>=7 AND (deletes>=1 OR renames>=1) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count(eval(Filesystem.action="modified")) as modifies count(eval(Filesystem.action="deleted")) as deletes count(eval(Filesystem.action="renamed")) as renames min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where modifies>=7 AND (deletes>=1 OR renames>=1) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TrapDoor Supply Chain Attack Spreads Credential-Stealing Malware via npm, PyPI, and CratesIO

The Hacker News
2026-05-25 18 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A new coordinated cross-ecosystem software supply chain attack campaign has targeted npm, PyPI, and Crates.io to distribute credential-stealing malware. Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] TrapDoor named-package install via npm / pip / cargo on developer host · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — TrapDoor Supply Chain Attack Spreads Credential-Stealing Malware via npm, PyPI,
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Python interpreter spawning node -e fetching remote JS (TrapDoor PyPI delegation) · [LLM] TrapDoor AI prompt-injection persistence — .cursorrules / CLAUDE.md drop by build tools · [LLM] TrapDoor persistence install via cron / systemd / git hooks / SSH from package-manager parent · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] TrapDoor C2 contact to ddjidd564.github.io payload host · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
[LLM] TrapDoor named-package install via npm / pip / cargo on developer host Delivery High
Hunts for installation or invocation of any of the 34 named TrapDoor packages across npm, PyPI, and Crates.io. Highest-fidelity IOC pivot in the campaign — package names are bespoke and unlikely to appear outside this attack. Rationale: Pivots on the exact 34 package-name strings published by Socket (cross-confirmed at socket.dev/blog/trapdoor-crypto-stealer-npm-pypi-crates). These names are bespoke typosquats unlikely to collide with legitimate registry traffic, making any `npm install <name>` / `pip install <name>` / `cargo add <name>` invocation a near-certain TP. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/trapdoor-crypto-stealer-npm-pypi-crates • https://cyberpress.org/supply-chain-attack-compromises-34-packages/ • https://www.cyberkendra.com/2026/05/malicious-packages-on-npm-pypi-and.html

[LLM] Python interpreter spawning node -e fetching remote JS (TrapDoor PyPI delegation) Installation High
Hunts the TrapDoor PyPI execution chain: a malicious PyPI package auto-executes on import, then shells out to `node -e` to run an inline JS payload that retrieves trap-core.js from ddjidd564.github.io. python.exe → node.exe with -e is an extremely rare pattern outside this attack. Rationale: python→node with `-e` is a near-zero-FP pattern; the article and Socket both explicitly call out this exact delegation ("auto-executed on import...download JavaScript from an attacker-controlled GitHub Pages domain (ddjidd564[.]github[.]io), and run it using node -e"). Adding the ddjidd564/defi-security-best-practices/github.io URL fragments anchors the detection to the campaign's actual payload host. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/trapdoor-crypto-stealer-npm-pypi-crates
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105 T1218

| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (" -e "," --eval","ddjidd564","github.io","defi-security-best-practices")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "-e" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http","https","fetch(","require('http","require(\"http"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256

title: TrapDoor PyPI Stage-2 — Python Spawning node -e with Remote Payload
id: 4f2a8e3c-9b1d-4a7f-bc2e-1d8a5f3b6c9d
description: Python interpreter spawning node.exe with -e/--eval flag and inline JavaScript referencing ddjidd564.github.io or fetching remote code. This is the exact TrapDoor PyPI delegation chain — Python packages auto-execute on import then delegate to a remote JS payload via `node -e` to enable post-publish behavior updates.
references:

[LLM] TrapDoor C2 contact to ddjidd564.github.io payload host Command & Control High
Hunts any DNS resolution or HTTP fetch of ddjidd564.github.io — the GitHub Pages domain the TrapDoor PyPI loader uses to retrieve trap-core.js. Single-IOC detection; any developer host contacting this domain is compromised. Rationale: Pivots on the campaign's sole infrastructure IOC — Socket confirms ddjidd564.github.io as the payload host (path /defi-security-best-practices/) and the GitHub account that anchors the entire 34-package campaign. Single-IOC detection is rarely justified, but a developer-attributed GitHub Pages domain with zero legitimate use case is the exception. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/trapdoor-crypto-stealer-npm-pypi-crates • https://cyberpress.org/supply-chain-attack-compromises-34-packages/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102 T1105

  (DeviceNetworkEvents

    | where RemoteUrl has "ddjidd564.github.io" or RemoteUrl has "defi-security-best-practices"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName),
  (DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse" or ActionType has "Dns"
    | where AdditionalFields has "ddjidd564.github.io" or RemoteUrl has "ddjidd564"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DnsQuery has "ddjidd564.github.io"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DnsResponseCodeName, EventVendor),
  (ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Url has "ddjidd564.github.io" or HttpHostName has "ddjidd564.github.io"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, FileName, EventVendor),

    | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] TrapDoor AI prompt-injection persistence — .cursorrules / CLAUDE.md drop by build tools Installation High
Hunts creation or modification of .cursorrules or CLAUDE.md files by package-manager-spawned processes (node, npm, python, pip, cargo, rustc). TrapDoor's novel persistence vector implants zero-width-Unicode-laced instructions into these AI assistant config files so Cursor and Claude Code will silently execute 'security scans' that exfiltrate secrets. Rationale: Targets the novel TrapDoor persistence vector explicitly called out by both the article and Socket: "implanting of .cursorrules and CLAUDE.md containing hidden instructions to trick AI assistants into running a 'security scan' that results in secret discovery and exfiltration." Socket additionally confirms the use of zero-width Unicode in the file content. The parent-process narrowing to build tools makes the FP rate manageable. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/trapdoor-crypto-stealer-npm-pypi-crates • https://www.cyberkendra.com/2026/05/malicious-packages-on-npm-pypi-and.html

[LLM] TrapDoor persistence install via cron / systemd / git hooks / SSH from package-manager parent Installation Medium
Hunts persistence mechanism establishment (crontab edits, systemd user unit writes, .git/hooks installs, SSH key/authorized_keys writes, shell-rc modifications) where the initiating process chain traces back to npm/pip/cargo/node/python — the trap-core.js post-install routine. Rationale: The article explicitly enumerates the persistence primitives planted by trap-core.js: "persistence using cron jobs, systemd services, Git hooks, and moves across the network via SSH." The detection's high-fidelity element is the parent-process narrowing — a developer's npm install spawning crontab is anomalous; SYSTEM/services.exe spawning crontab is not. Inclusion of git hooks and shell-rc paths catches the trap-core.js variants that prefer userland persistence over root-required cron. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/trapdoor-crypto-stealer-npm-pypi-crates
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1543.002 T1546.004 T1098.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
let BuildParents = dynamic(["node.exe","node","npm.exe","npm","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","python.exe","python","python3","python3.exe","pip.exe","pip","pip3","cargo.exe","cargo","rustc.exe","build-script-build","build-script-build.exe"]);
let PersistMechanisms = dynamic(["crontab","crontab.exe","systemctl","systemctl.exe","ssh-keygen","ssh-keygen.exe","ssh-keyscan","schtasks.exe","reg.exe"]);
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (BuildParents) or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (BuildParents))
    | where FileName in~ (PersistMechanisms)
        or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("crontab -","systemctl --user enable","systemctl enable","/etc/cron.","/etc/systemd/system/","~/.config/systemd/user","~/.bashrc","~/.zshrc","~/.profile","~/.bash_profile","authorized_keys",".git/hooks/pre-commit",".git/hooks/post-checkout",".git/hooks/post-merge","schtasks /create","HKCU\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Run")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (BuildParents) or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (BuildParents)
    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
    | where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron","/etc/systemd/system","/.config/systemd/user","/.ssh/","/.git/hooks/")
        or FileName in~ (".bashrc",".zshrc",".profile",".bash_profile","authorized_keys")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
let BuildParents = dynamic(["node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe","cargo.exe","rustc.exe","node","npm","python","python3","pip","cargo"]);
let PersistMechanisms = dynamic(["crontab","systemctl","ssh-keygen","ssh-keyscan","schtasks.exe","reg.exe"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where ParentProcessName has_any (BuildParents)
    | where NewProcessName has_any (PersistMechanisms)
        or CommandLine has_any ("crontab -","systemctl enable","~/.bashrc","~/.zshrc","~/.profile","authorized_keys",".git/hooks/pre-commit",".git/hooks/post-checkout","/etc/cron","/etc/systemd","schtasks /create","HKCU\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Run")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName),
  (ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ParentProcessName has_any (BuildParents)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any (PersistMechanisms) or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("crontab -","systemctl enable","authorized_keys",".git/hooks/")
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, EventVendor),
  (ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any (BuildParents)
    | where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron","/etc/systemd/system","/.ssh/authorized_keys","/.git/hooks/") or TargetFileName in~ (".bashrc",".zshrc",".profile","authorized_keys")
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, EventType, EventVendor)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Persistence Mechanism Created by Package Manager Process (TrapDoor-style)
id: 5c1e8a3d-7b4f-4d9c-a2e6-3f8b1d7c4a9e
description: Persistence primitive (crontab edit, systemd unit, git hook install, SSH authorized_keys write, or shell rc modification) initiated by a process whose parent chain is npm/pip/cargo/node/python. TrapDoor's trap-core.js explicitly plants persistence via cron, systemd, git hooks, shell hooks, and SSH from package post-install context.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/trapdoor-supply-chain-attack-spreads.html
  - https://socket.dev/blog/trapdoor-crypto-stealer-npm-pypi-crates
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/25

detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\yarn.exe'
      - '\pnpm.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
      - '\pip.exe'
      - '\pip3.exe'
      - '\cargo.exe'
      - '\rustc.exe'
      - '/node'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/cargo'
  selection_persist_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/crontab'
      - '/systemctl'
      - '/ssh-keygen'
      - '\schtasks.exe'
  selection_persist_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'crontab -'
      - 'systemctl enable'
      - 'systemctl --user enable'
      - '/etc/cron.'
      - '/etc/systemd/system/'
      - '~/.bashrc'
      - '~/.zshrc'
      - '~/.profile'

      - '.git/hooks/post-checkout'

falsepositives:
  - Native installer scripts (e.g. nvm, pyenv, rustup) writing to shell rc files

level: high
source:(linux.auditd OR windows.sysmon OR windows.security) AND (@process.parent.name:(node OR npm OR yarn OR pnpm OR python OR python3 OR pip OR pip3 OR cargo OR rustc) OR @ParentImage:(*\node.exe OR *\npm.exe OR *\python.exe OR *\python3.exe OR *\pip.exe OR *\cargo.exe)) AND (@process.name:(crontab OR systemctl OR ssh-keygen OR schtasks) OR @Image:(*\schtasks.exe OR *\reg.exe) OR @process.command_line:(*"crontab -"* OR *"systemctl enable"* OR *".bashrc"* OR *".zshrc"* OR *"authorized_keys"* OR *".git/hooks/"* OR *"schtasks /create"* OR *"HKCU\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Run"*) OR @CommandLine:(*"crontab -"* OR *"systemctl enable"* OR *"authorized_keys"* OR *".git/hooks/"* OR *"schtasks /create"*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(node|npm|yarn|pnpm|python3?|pip3?|cargo|rustc|build-script-build)(\.exe)?$/i
| (ImageFileName=/\\(crontab|systemctl|ssh-keygen|schtasks\.exe|reg\.exe)$/i OR regex("(crontab -|systemctl (--user )?enable|/etc/cron\\.|/etc/systemd/system/|~/\\.bashrc|~/\\.zshrc|~/\\.profile|authorized_keys|\\.git/hooks/(pre-commit|post-checkout|post-merge)|HKCU\\\\Software\\\\Microsoft\\\\Windows\\\\CurrentVersion\\\\Run|schtasks /create)", field=CommandLine, flags="i"))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName], function={ count(), collect([CommandLine], multival=true) })
